title: Cause and effect: did it actually work?
hook: Correlation, A/B tests, comparison groups, matching, and finding who really responds.
inPlainWords: A model can show that two things move together without showing that one causes the other. To know whether a discount caused a sale, you need a comparison that would have looked the same without the discount.

useCase.title: Did the 10% coupon email cause more purchases?
useCase.story: Customers who received the coupon email bought 30% more than those who did not. But the coupon was sent mostly to loyal customers who already buy a lot. The team wants to know the real effect, and who benefits most.

approaches.name: Compare the groups as they are
approaches.what: Compare buyers who got the coupon with those who did not.
approaches.avoidWhen: The groups differ in ways that matter.
approaches.example: The coupon group bought 30% more, but they were the loyal ones.

approaches.name: Randomized A/B test
approaches.what: Randomly choose who gets the coupon.
approaches.avoidWhen: Randomizing is unethical, illegal or impractical.

approaches.name: Before and after
approaches.what: Compare the same customers before and after.
approaches.example: Sales rose after the campaign, and they rise every December.

approaches.name: Comparison group over time
approaches.what: Compare the change in one group with the change in a similar untreated group.
approaches.greatWhen: You cannot randomize, but a similar group exists.
approaches.avoidWhen: The groups were already on different trends.
approaches.example: A coupon region against a similar no-coupon region.

approaches.name: Matching or adjusting
approaches.what: Compare customers who look alike except for the coupon.
approaches.greatWhen: You have rich data on why people got it.
approaches.example: Match on past spend, region and visits.

approaches.name: Uplift modeling
approaches.what: Model who changes behavior because of the treatment.
approaches.greatWhen: You have randomized data and want to target well.
approaches.example: Find customers who buy only if they get the coupon.

challenge.question: How do you find the coupon's true effect, and who it works on?

options.text: Randomly hold back a group in the next send, compare, then model who responds most
options.why: Randomness makes the groups comparable, so the difference is caused by the coupon.

options.text: Compare coupon and no-coupon customers from last month
options.why: Loyal customers got the coupon, so the comparison is unfair.

options.text: Treat the model's top predictors as causes

options.why: A useful sanity check, but seasons and trends confuse it.

bestCase.title: A fair comparison, then target who responds
bestCase.example: A random 10% hold-out shows the coupon adds 4% more purchases, not 30%. An uplift model finds that occasional buyers respond strongly while loyal customers would have bought anyway. Future coupons go to the responders and margin improves.

worstCase.title: Mistaking correlation for cause
worstCase.example: The team sees 30% more purchases among coupon recipients and sends the coupon to everyone. Most would have bought anyway, so margin falls while sales barely change.

steps.label: Randomize
steps.goes: A coin flip decides who gets the coupon.
steps.goesWrong: The coupon goes to the loyal customers who already buy.

steps.label: Send and wait
steps.goes: Two weeks of purchases are recorded.

steps.label: Compare the groups
steps.goes: The extra sales are caused by the coupon, not by who got it.

steps.label: Model who responds
steps.goes: An uplift model finds who really changes behavior.

steps.label: Target and re-test
steps.goes: Send to responders, and keep testing.

takeaway: Correlation shows what moves together. Only a fair comparison, ideally a randomized one, shows what a change causes.
